title: Graph Tables
description: Model nodes and edges with SQL Server graph tables and traverse relationships with MATCH.

data.text: SQL Server 2017 added graph tables for many-to-many relationships that are awkward to model with junction tables. A node table represents entities; an edge table represents relationships between nodes. Under the hood they are still tables with hidden columns (`$node_id`, `$edge_id`, `$from_id`, `$to_id`), so they participate in transactions, backups, and security like any other table. The `MATCH` predicate expresses traversal patterns that would otherwise need recursive CTEs.

data.caption: Person nodes are connected by Friend edges; each edge stores the relationship attributes and references its two endpoint nodes.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    P1["Person\nAda"] -->|Friend since 2024| P2["Person\nGrace"]
    P2 -->|Friend since 2023| P3["Person\nAlan"]
    P1 -->|Friend since 2022| P3
    P1 --- N1["NODE table dbo.Person"]
    P2 --- N1
    P3 --- N1
    E1["EDGE table dbo.Friend\nSince"] --- P1
    E1 --- P2

data.text: Node tables use `AS NODE`; edge tables use `AS EDGE`. You can add ordinary columns to both. Edge tables can also have edge constraints (SQL Server 2019+) that restrict which node tables an edge may connect.

data.title: Person nodes and Friend edges
data.content: Insert nodes first, then insert edges by selecting the generated `$node_id` values from the node table.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE dbo.Person
(
    PersonId INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    Name     NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
) AS NODE;
GO

CREATE TABLE dbo.Friend
(
    Since DATE NULL
) AS EDGE;
GO

INSERT INTO dbo.Person (PersonId, Name)
VALUES (1, N'Ada'), (2, N'Grace'), (3, N'Alan');

INSERT INTO dbo.Friend ($from_id, $to_id, Since)
SELECT p1.$node_id, p2.$node_id, '2024-01-01'
FROM dbo.Person AS p1
JOIN dbo.Person AS p2
    ON p2.PersonId = 2
WHERE p1.PersonId = 1;

INSERT INTO dbo.Friend ($from_id, $to_id, Since)
SELECT p1.$node_id, p2.$node_id, '2022-06-15'
FROM dbo.Person AS p1
JOIN dbo.Person AS p2
    ON p2.PersonId = 3
WHERE p1.PersonId = 1;

data.title: Direct friends and friends of friends
data.content: The first query returns Ada's direct friends. The second chains two edge patterns to reach friends of friends.
data.code:
-- Direct friends
SELECT
    p1.Name AS person,
    p2.Name AS friend,
    f.Since
FROM dbo.Person AS p1, dbo.Friend AS f, dbo.Person AS p2
WHERE MATCH(p1-(f)->p2)
  AND p1.PersonId = 1;

-- Friends of friends
SELECT
    p1.Name AS person,
    p3.Name AS friend_of_friend
FROM dbo.Person AS p1,
     dbo.Friend AS f1,
     dbo.Person AS p2,
     dbo.Friend AS f2,
     dbo.Person AS p3
WHERE MATCH(p1-(f1)->p2-(f2)->p3)
  AND p1.PersonId = 1
  AND p3.PersonId <> p1.PersonId;

data.title: SHORTEST_PATH and edge constraints
data.text: `MATCH` supports `SHORTEST_PATH` for shortest-path queries between two nodes, and SQL Server 2019 added edge constraints so an edge table can only connect specific node tables. Both features are useful, but they change how the optimizer plans the query — test with realistic graph sizes.

data.title: Interview angle: graph tables vs a junction table
data.text: A junction table plus recursive CTE can model the same relationships and is often simpler for fixed-depth queries. Graph tables become attractive when relationships are first-class (multiple edge types and attributes), when queries traverse variable-depth paths, and when you want the traversal expressed declaratively. They are not a graph database: there is no distributed traversal engine, and deep traversals can still be expensive.

data.title: Graph Tables Key Points
points: Node tables use AS NODE; edge tables use AS EDGE and carry the relationship attributes.
Insert edges by selecting the node ids from the node table.
MATCH expresses traversal patterns with a visual arrow syntax.
Chained MATCH patterns and SHORTEST_PATH handle multi-hop queries.
Graph tables are still tables: they participate in transactions, backups, and security.
